The quarry that became a battery

By Ffion Rhys · 11 May 2026 · Infrastructure

The road out of Llanberis climbs past the lake and then stops caring about the lake entirely. It turns inland, into a valley that was quarried so thoroughly for so long that the hillside now reads as architecture rather than geology: forty terraces cut in steps, each one wide enough for a narrow-gauge railway, each one backed by a face of blue-grey slate that still splits along the cleavage planes the Cambrian gave it half a billion years ago. From the far shore the terraces look like the seating of an amphitheatre built for something enormous. In a sense that is exactly what they are.

Between 1780 and 1969 the quarry above Llanberis produced roofing slate for most of northern Europe. At its height it employed three thousand men and cut through the mountain at a rate of a terrace a decade. The men worked in bargeins, small partnerships that bid for a stretch of rock and were paid on what they could split out of it, which meant that the quarry was never a single machine but several hundred small businesses arranged vertically on a cliff. Then the market for slate collapsed, twice, and in 1969 the last shift walked out and the pumps were switched off.

What happened next is the part that interests engineers. The quarry did not simply close. It filled. Rainwater and groundwater found the lowest galleries and stayed there, and by the mid-1970s the bottom third of the workings had become a lake with a very unusual shape: deep, cold, entirely enclosed by rock, and sitting several hundred metres below another body of water that the quarrymen had left behind on the plateau above. Two reservoirs, one on top of the other, separated by a vertical distance that nature would have taken a geological age to arrange and that men with black powder and crowbars had produced in under two centuries.

A pumped-storage plant is the oldest idea in grid-scale energy storage and still the largest. You need two bodies of water at different heights and a tunnel between them. When there is more electricity on the network than anyone wants, you run the machines as pumps and move water uphill. When there is less, you let it fall back through the same machines, now acting as turbines, and put the electricity back. The round trip costs you a quarter of what you started with, and in exchange you get something no battery chemistry has yet matched at scale: a store that can be built to hold six hours of national demand and that will still be doing the same job in eighty years.

The physics is unforgiving in a way that makes it easy to reason about. The energy in the upper reservoir is the mass of the water times gravity times the head, and nothing about that expression can be improved by cleverness. You can only push on two terms. Head is the one that pays: doubling the vertical drop doubles the stored energy for the same volume of water and the same excavation. Which is why pumped storage is built in mountains, and why a mountain that has already been hollowed out by somebody else is worth a great deal of money.

The Llanberis scheme, when it was finally consented, took the upper quarry lake as its head pond and the lake in the valley floor as its tail. The gross head is four hundred and forty metres. The tunnel between them is nine metres in diameter for most of its length and narrows into six penstocks in the last four hundred metres, where the water arrives at the machine hall at fifty metres a second, which is fast enough that the steel liner has to be thicker than the rock it is holding back.

The machine hall itself is inside the mountain, in a cavern that is the largest man-made chamber in Europe by volume and one of the quietest places any of the engineers who work there have ever stood. It is one hundred and eighty metres long, twenty-four wide, and sixty from floor to crown, and when all six units are stopped the loudest thing in it is the ventilation. When they are running the noise is not what a visitor expects either. It is not a roar. It is a very low, very even hum, felt in the sternum before it is heard, that does not change pitch or volume for hours at a time.

Each of the six units is a reversible Francis machine coupled to a motor-generator that weighs four hundred tonnes. Reversible is doing a lot of work in that sentence. A turbine and a pump are not the same machine run backwards; the blade geometry that extracts energy efficiently from falling water is not the geometry that adds energy to rising water, and every reversible unit ever built is a compromise between the two. The compromise costs about three percentage points of efficiency in each direction, and the industry has decided, correctly, that three points is cheaper than two separate machine halls.

The number the operators care about most is not efficiency, though. It is time. A plant like this exists to be somewhere else on the demand curve within seconds, and the specification it was built against is twelve seconds from standstill to full output. The way that is achieved is a trick worth describing, because it is entirely mechanical and completely at odds with how people imagine a modern grid works.

Before a unit is needed, it is spun up to synchronous speed in air rather than water. Compressed air is blown into the turbine casing, pushing the water level down below the runner, so the machine is turning at five hundred revolutions a minute in an air pocket, drawing almost no power and generating none. This is called spinning in air, or, in the control room, being on standby. From that state the operators need only open the guide vanes and let the water back in. The machine is already synchronised to the grid, already at speed, already in phase; there is nothing left to do but load it.

The rest of the twelve seconds is spent on the water column. There are half a million tonnes of it in the shaft and the tunnel, and it has to be accelerated from rest. That acceleration is the thing that limits the response, and it is also the thing that produces the plant's most dangerous failure mode. If the guide vanes close quickly on a moving column, the column does not stop. It compresses, and the pressure wave that comes back up the tunnel can exceed the static head by half again. Every pumped-storage scheme in the world is built around some device for absorbing that wave, and at Llanberis it is a surge shaft: a vertical chamber, sixty metres tall, that the water is allowed to run up into and slosh back down out of over a period of several minutes.

The surge shaft is the reason the plant can be closed suddenly at all, and it is also the reason the plant is not quite as fast as the twelve-second figure suggests. Twelve seconds is the time to full output from spinning in air. From a genuine cold start, with the machines stopped and the tunnel drained of momentum, it is closer to two minutes. Both numbers are true, and both get quoted, and the difference between them explains most of the arguments about what pumped storage is actually for.

The economic case has changed shape three times since the plant was consented. It was built for a grid dominated by large thermal plant that could not be turned down quickly, and its original job was to absorb overnight nuclear output and sell it back at the evening peak — a straightforward arbitrage on a demand curve that was, in the 1970s, extremely predictable. That job largely evaporated when the thermal fleet shrank. For a decade the plant made most of its money from frequency response, holding the network at fifty hertz by injecting or absorbing power on a timescale of seconds, which is a service it can provide better than almost anything else connected to the system.

Now the job has changed again. The variable that dominates the British grid is wind, and wind does not follow a curve that anyone can publish a day ahead with confidence. On a windy Sunday night in February the network can find itself with more generation than load, and the cheapest thing to do with the surplus is to pay somebody to take it. The plant takes it, moves half a million tonnes of water four hundred and forty metres uphill, and waits. Sometimes it waits four hours. Occasionally, in a still week, it waits eleven days.

That waiting is the awkward part of the economics, and it is why so few schemes have been built since. A pumped-storage plant is almost entirely capital. The water is free, the mountain is free, the marginal cost of a cycle is close to nothing, and essentially the whole lifetime cost was incurred before the first unit turned. Financing that against a revenue stream set by the volatility of a market twenty years out is a proposition that no private developer has been able to make work in Britain without a contract that guarantees a floor, and the argument about who should write that contract has now been running for longer than the plant took to build.

The engineering, meanwhile, has aged extremely well. The civil works — the cavern, the tunnel, the shafts — were specified for a hundred and twenty years and there is no evidence so far that the specification was pessimistic. Rock is not a material that fatigues in any way a human timescale can detect, and the parts that do wear are the parts that were always meant to be replaced. The runners have been changed once. The motor-generators have been rewound. The control system has been replaced three times, and the third replacement removed more cable than the first installation contained.

What has not aged well is the assumption embedded in the original design that the plant would run two cycles a day, on a schedule known in advance. It now runs whenever the market says so, which in practice means far more starts and far shorter runs. Starts are what damage a machine of this kind. Each one puts the runner through a thermal and mechanical transient that a steady four-hour run does not, and the maintenance interval, which used to be counted in years, is now counted in starts. The plant has performed more starts in the last five years than in its first twenty.

This is the quiet story of the energy transition, told through a single asset: nothing about the hardware failed, and everything about the duty cycle changed. The same is true of the interconnectors, of the remaining thermal fleet, and of the distribution network in every town that has installed more solar than its transformers were sized for. The grid was designed as a machine for moving power from a few large places to many small ones, on a schedule, and it is now being asked to be a machine for balancing many small places against each other, continuously, at a notice of seconds.

Back on the surface the terraces are being colonised. The lower ones, where the spoil is finest, have gone to birch and rowan. Higher up, where there is nothing but broken slate, there is a lichen flora that botanists from three countries come to look at, and a population of choughs that nest in the old drill holes. The quarry buildings that survive have been converted twice, first into a museum and then into a climbing centre, and the incline that once lowered loaded wagons to the lakeside is now a footpath with an interpretation board at the bottom explaining what a bargein was.

None of this is visible from the machine hall. Six hundred metres of rock is an effective divider between a landscape and an industrial process, and the men and women who run the plant spend their shifts in a room with no windows, watching a schematic of a mountain they cannot see. The schematic is not to scale. It has never needed to be. What matters in that room is the level in the upper pond, the position of six sets of guide vanes, and the frequency of a network that is, at any given second, either slightly fast or slightly slow, and never exactly right.

The plant answers that question about eight hundred times a day. It is the oldest kind of storage there is, in the oldest kind of hole, doing the newest job on the system, and it will still be doing it when everything currently described as a grid battery has been recycled twice. There is a lesson in that about durability, and about the value of infrastructure that was built for one purpose by people who had no idea what the next purpose would be. Mostly, though, there is a lesson about heads: that the single most valuable thing anyone ever did for the British electricity system was to spend two centuries digging a very deep hole in Snowdonia for an entirely unrelated reason.
